title: Who Decides Zero Trust for the Whole Agency?
say: Welcome. This is the executive briefing for Book 11 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Zero Trust and Assessment. It runs about thirty minutes, and it's for the people who make the calls: the CISO, the authorizing officials, the CIO, and the Zero Trust implementation lead. The argument fits in three sentences. Zero Trust maturity is a property of the whole agency, not of any product or tenant. The federal documents set specific actions and configurations, but none of them defines a Zero Trust score or requires a maturity stage. And the assessment tools produce evidence for named people to act on, not verdicts to report. I'll take four questions in order: why Zero Trust belongs to the whole agency, what the mandates and tools actually require, who owns the posture, and how to turn findings into a program the authorizing official can see. Every decision slide names the decision, its owner, and when it's needed. Let's start with the usual assessment calendar.

title: Three reports stapled together are not one score
say: Here's how assessment usually works. The network team reviews the boundary, keyed by address. The cloud team runs each provider's posture scan, keyed by resource tags. The virtualization team works a hypervisor checklist. At year end someone puts the three reports behind one cover page and calls it the agency's Zero Trust maturity. It's three partial assessments with one title. The failure is architectural, not organizational. A policy decision can only treat a user, a device and a resource consistently if every platform describes them the same way. One database server can show up as three unrelated objects, scored by three tools. A total across them counts objects, not architecture. The federal guidance describes the enterprise, not a tenant. Executive Order 14028, M-22-09, CISA's maturity model and NIST all speak in agency-wide terms. A scan can confirm that an architecture is unified; it can't make it unified. So the first decision: reconcile the network, every cloud and the virtualization estate to one authoritative asset and identity record before scoring any of them. The book gives that to the owner of the naming and identity plane, this quarter. Until it's done, report any whole-agency figure as partial assessments, not one score. Next, why this is a security issue, not a reporting preference.

title: The worst failures sat beneath any one tool
say: Two documented incidents show why this is a security property and not a reporting preference. In 2023, an attacker used a Microsoft consumer signing key to forge tokens and read Exchange Online mail. The Cyber Safety Review Board counted 22 enterprise organizations affected, and called the intrusion preventable. The forged tokens were valid to every system that checked them. What caught it was a custom alert one federal department had built on mailbox logs it paid for. The agency's own evidence found what the provider's platform didn't. The second sits beneath the guest. In February 2023, the ESXiArgs campaign compromised more than 3,800 VMware ESXi servers. And Microsoft noted that many security products have limited visibility into the hypervisor at all. Both cases make the same point from opposite ends. The worst failures happened where no single platform's tool was looking. There's a consequence for the fix, too. Once one plane names and identifies everything the agency runs, it's a complete map of the attack surface. So the decision: govern that unified plane as a Tier 0 asset from the day it exists, with time-boxed administration, its own monitored telemetry, and a design that assumes it will be attacked. Identity engineering and the DNS and DDI team own it. Next, why programs stall.

title: Maturity is decided by governance, which nobody sells
say: Programs stall low on CISA's maturity model because they read it as a five-pillar shopping list: identity, devices, networks, applications and data. But the model runs those pillars through three cross-cutting capabilities, and the one programs fund least is governance: defining and enforcing policy across pillars. No single pillar's tool delivers that. Three failure patterns recur. Pillars are administered, not governed. Evidence is shaped by each tool rather than by the claim it supports, so every assessment starts from scratch. And drift is found at audit time, months after it opened. The book's answer rests on a few principles. Identity is the anchor, but it isn't self-authenticating, so sessions are re-evaluated and the identity plane is defended. Privileged identity gets controls of its own. Evidence must be reproducible and machine-readable. And governance must enforce, not only observe. A policy whose only consequence is next quarter's finding is a report. The decision is the CISO's, with identity engineering, this quarter: time-box privileged access, including the assessment accounts, and convert one detective control into a preventive one. Microsoft's own guidance is zero permanently active admin assignments, other than emergency accounts that are monitored and tested at least every 90 days. Next, what the mandates actually require.

title: Only one Zero Trust document sets requirements
say: Zero Trust programs are usually argued by citation, and most of the citations fail when you check them. Four documents get cited as if they were one. Executive Order 14028 is binding, and required each agency to plan for Zero Trust Architecture. OMB M-22-09 is binding, and sets specific actions by pillar. CISA's maturity model is guidance; it says it shouldn't be viewed as a strict set of requirements, and its page is now marked archived. NIST SP 800-207 is guidance too. M-22-09 borrows the model's pillars to organize its actions, but doesn't adopt its stages as requirements. That leaves several requirements that circulate but don't exist. No federal document requires a particular maturity stage, such as Advanced. No federal document defines a Zero Trust score, so a tool that claims to certify maturity is citing a requirement that isn't there. And M-22-09 doesn't require ScubaGear; that comes from BOD 25-01. None of that makes the target vague. It means the target is a choice the agency makes and has to defend. So the decision: set a maturity target for each pillar, written down as program design, not mandate. The Zero Trust program lead decides it, consulting the CIO, the CISO and the authorizing official, before the next assessment is scored. Next, the one memo that still binds.

title: M-22-09 still binds: read it as an existing obligation
say: M-22-09 is the only one of these that sets dated actions for the program itself, and it isn't limited to the cloud. It covers on-premises and hybrid systems too. Its actions are specific. Phishing-resistant MFA for staff, contractors and partners, which means agency systems stop supporting SMS and voice codes, one-time codes and push notifications for routine access. Reliable device inventories and endpoint detection. Encrypted DNS, HTTPS for all web and API traffic, and moving away from one broad enterprise network. Security testing for applications, and comprehensive logging. Its fiscal 2024 deadlines have passed. But OMB hasn't rescinded it, and a passed deadline doesn't retire an action. Agencies are now measured against these actions as an existing obligation rather than a target date. There's one adjustment. The logging action pointed to M-21-31, which M-26-14 rescinded on May 22, 2026, replacing it with a risk-based approach and a Logging Reference Architecture. CISA published that architecture on August 20, 2026, and agencies have 90 days from its release for their first Agency Logging Plan. That's the decision with the nearest date. The CISO decides how the logging plan covers Zero Trust telemetry, including the hosts and accounts that run the assessments. It's due 90 days after August 20, 2026. Next, BOD 25-01.

title: BOD 25-01: six actions, and the half that matters
say: BOD 25-01 is narrower and more concrete. CISA issued it on December 17, 2024, and it binds federal civilian agencies for every production cloud tenant of a product with a finalized SCuBA baseline. It has six required actions, from inventorying tenants and deploying the assessment tools to implementing the mandatory policies by June 20, 2025, and baselining every new tenant before its authorization to operate. The mandatory list is a subset of the baselines: 50 policies for Microsoft 365. And the scope is software as a service only, so Azure subscriptions, on-premises Active Directory, endpoints and networks are untouched. Google Workspace is now in scope. Its tenant inventory is due November 2, 2026, and the tools by December 1. CISA's pages disagree on the policy date, so plan to December 1. Even a small tenant used by one component carries all six obligations. Now count honestly. Inventory and reporting take days. Implementing and holding the policies is architecture, and that's what the directive exists for. So measure compliance by how many mandatory policies hold, and whether every open deviation is either being fixed on a date or carried as the authorizing official's documented risk acceptance. The CISO owns the inventory and reporting, and the Workspace inventory is due November 2. Next, reporting.

title: Reporting to CISA, and where deviations go
say: Reporting is where many agencies stopped, so it's worth being precise about what CISA actually receives. CISA's guidance describes four reporting routes, from a CISA-hosted service that feeds the CDM dashboard to quarterly manual uploads. Whatever the route, the reported artifact is the tool's own results file, and agencies are told not to rename it. A deviation that's operationally required shows up as Omitted, with its rationale, and must be approved through the agency's security risk process. CISA also supplies a template for tracking non-compliant policies, planned fixes and target dates. In effect, it's a plan of action and milestones. The directive puts the risk decision in the right place. Authorizing officials may accept risk for deviations from the mandatory policies to meet operational needs, under agency policy, and CISA reviews what they submit. Two decisions follow. The CISO picks the reporting route, and the assessment operators run it. Operators never edit results, and never decide omissions. And every deviation without an end date goes to the authorizing official, because a standing omission is a standing risk acceptance. The reporting floor is at least quarterly, so both are needed before the next quarterly report. Next, the two assessment tools.

title: Two assessment tools, two questions, no verdict
say: Agencies can run two free, read-only assessments of their Microsoft cloud, and often drop one because both cover identity. They answer different questions. ScubaGear is CISA's tool. It asks a compliance question: does this Microsoft 365 tenant meet the federal baselines? It's the tool the directive names, and its output is what CISA receives. Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment asks a maturity question: how close is the environment to Microsoft's own guidance? It's a community project maintained by Microsoft employees, not an official product, and it isn't a BOD 25-01 tool. They overlap mostly on identity. Only ScubaGear covers Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint and Power Platform, where 22 of the 50 mandatory policies sit. Drop ScubaGear and mandatory policies go unassessed and the required reporting stops. Drop the other, and devices, network and data go unmeasured. Even running both is one vendor's answer about one vendor's platform. Neither sees another cloud, the network or the hypervisors. And a score is a reading, not a treatment plan. The CISO decides, before the next production run: approve both tools, with pinned versions, and keep their output inside the authorization boundary, because it's a map of where the tenant is weak. Expect the score to move when a version changes, even if the tenant didn't. Next, everything beyond Microsoft 365.

title: Beyond Microsoft 365, each tool answers for itself
say: Everything so far stops at the edge of Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. Nothing on BOD 25-01's list covers infrastructure accounts, the agency network or the virtualized estate. So the whole-agency argument rests on the Zero Trust documents, and on the controls every system security plan already asserts. Three things get reconciled before those estates are assessed. One inventory, with no component counted twice. One naming authority, because each cloud provider and VMware ships its own private DNS. And no implicit trust from any boundary: a site-to-site VPN and a flat virtualized segment are architecturally the same mistake. The hypervisor is a threat class of its own, so its management plane is assessed as its own surface. Then the providers' own tools, each of which states its own limits. AWS says its checks cover a subset of requirements. Microsoft calls Azure Policy compliance a partial view. Broadcom calls its VMware hardening material general guidance. And FedRAMP certifies the cloud service, while each agency still authorizes its own systems. The decision is the program lead's: admit each native tool's findings as evidence for its own platform, under the CISO's evidence standard, and never as the agency's score. It's needed before any whole-agency figure is reported. Next, who owns the posture.

title: Every pillar has an owner; the posture needs one too
say: Zero Trust programs rarely fail for lack of owners. They fail because every owner is a pillar owner. Nobody owns the question this book keeps asking: what is the agency's posture across all five pillars, and what does the number on the cover page actually measure? The CIO and executive sponsor set strategy, scope and funding, and break ties. Three CIO decisions matter here: which estates the whole-agency score covers, in writing, so it can't quietly shrink to the estates that assess well; the sequence of work; and which team owns a control that spans pillars. The Zero Trust program lead owns the posture: the definition of the score, the assessment calendar and the prioritized worklist. Many agencies will give this to the implementation lead M-22-09 required. The lead decides priority but doesn't accept risk, and shouldn't also own the agency's relationship with its largest cloud vendor. That independence is the point of the role. The CISO sets the evidence standard, and the authorizing officials accept residual risk, each only for the systems they authorize. The decision is the CIO's, this quarter: name an agency-level owner of the Zero Trust posture, and a cross-pillar correlation owner, separate from any cloud provider relationship. Next, the pillar owners.

title: Who owns each pillar, and three calls that go astray
say: The book maps each of CISA's five pillars to the team that owns it after modernization: identity engineering, endpoint engineering, network engineering with security architecture, application owners with the platform teams, and the data owners. Across them, security operations owns visibility, and governance, the part no pillar owner can deliver alone, sits with the program lead, the CISO and the authorizing official. One rule runs through it. Pillar owners decide how to fix a finding. They don't decide that it doesn't need fixing. And three calls often land on the wrong desk. An exception with an expiration date is a CISO decision, recorded in the versioned configuration file. An exception with no end date is a standing risk acceptance, so it goes to the authorizing official, which matches BOD 25-01. And drift, a control that passed every interval and failed the last one, also goes to the authorizing official, because it's a change to an authorized system, and the official decides whether it's significant. So the decision for the CISO, this quarter: move every exception out of documents and into the configuration file and the repository, with an expiration, and route each standing one to the authorizing official. Next, how to get there.

title: Close before you assess: assessors run at step five
say: How do you get there? First, close before you assess. Agencies met BOD 25-01's early dates, with tenants inventoried and ScubaGear reporting, and many now treat that as the answer. But the tools measure deviation; they don't close any. A thermometer that reports a fever every day for a year isn't a treatment plan. Without an architecture to absorb the fix, remediation collapses into re-running the scan and filing another plan line. So the program's sequence puts the assessors at step five, as confirmation, not discovery: understand the gaps, design the fix, implement it, govern it, then validate, and then the authorizing official decides on the evidence. That's the Risk Management Framework's own order. Not every finding waits for architecture. Each gets exactly one response: a configuration change that closes now, architectural work with an owner and a date, or a risk acceptance by the authorizing official. A finding with no response recorded is the only state the program treats as failure. This is the CIO's sequence decision: close the BOD 25-01 findings before the maturity assessment, and staff that order against the agency's other deadlines. It's needed before the maturity assessment is scheduled. Next, how to read the results.

title: Read the result before you count it
say: The two tools use different words for the same outcomes, and some of their outcomes aren't findings at all. Only four results are findings: ScubaGear's Fail and Warning, and the Zero Trust Assessment's Failed and Investigate. The rest need care. A not-applicable result is usually a manual check to verify by hand, not a pass. An error means the run failed: fix it and re-run. And a skipped check is neither a gap nor a pass. Often the reason is a license, or a feature that isn't available or authorized in a government cloud. Scoring it as a failure overstates the gap; scoring it as a pass overstates the posture. So it's recorded as absence of evidence, with the reason, and it becomes a boundary finding. The program then ranks the real findings with a documented method, P1 down to P4. That method is the program's, not a federal standard, and a P1 is a priority, not a risk acceptance. And findings are reconciled at the control: two tools failing the same setting is one finding with two pieces of evidence, routed to one owner. Underneath it all sits the CISO's evidence standard: a pinned tool version, a recorded run time, an unaltered output file and a hash. It's needed before any result is scored or reported. Next, turning findings into a program.

title: From findings to a program the AO can see
say: Now turn the worklist into a program the authorizing official can see. Every finding that isn't fixed in the next change window and isn't covered by an approved exception becomes a plan of action and milestones item, which the authorizing official approves. Each item names the owner, the control, the evidence that will show it closed, and the re-assessment that will test it. Behind those items, the program seals each tool's unaltered output, with its provenance, into a bundle that rebuilds byte for byte. An assessor can rebuild it months later and walk back from a finding to the raw result. That's the difference between an archived opinion and evidence. Re-assessment runs on a calendar the program lead owns, and after each remediation wave, so a finding is closed by evidence, not by a ticket status. ScubaGear's floor is quarterly. And drift goes to the authorizing official, not only to security operations, because a control that newly fails is a change to an authorized system. The book calls that the cheapest adoption step in its final chapter. So the decision sits with the authorizing official: receive drift findings every assessment interval, prepared by the program lead and security operations, and decide which are significant changes. Stand it up this quarter. To close, the decisions in one place.

title: Decisions to make this quarter, and who makes them
say: So, the decisions, with their owners. None of them is a procurement. The CIO names an agency-level owner of the Zero Trust posture and a cross-pillar correlation owner, separate from any cloud provider relationship, and puts the scope of the whole-agency score in writing. The identity-plane owner reconciles the network, every cloud and the virtualization estate to one record before any is scored. The program lead finds out, pillar by pillar, which evidence can be re-run without the operator's help. The CISO moves every exception into the configuration file with an expiration, covers the assessment hosts and accounts in the Agency Logging Plan, due 90 days after August 20, brings any Google Workspace tenant into the inventory by November 2, and time-boxes privileged access. The program lead and security operations stand up drift detection, and the authorizing official receives its findings. And every government-cloud feature gap is recorded as a governed finding, not an unstated assumption. Each is a structural step that compounds. Unify first, assess second, and let named people make the decisions the evidence supports. No tool, and no number of tools, certifies Zero Trust maturity. Book 11 has the detail, with every claim footnoted. Thank you.
